report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is well supported. For pregnant people with chronic HBV and *high HBV DNA*—usually defined as ≥200,000 IU/mL (≥5.3 log10 IU/mL)—tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) started late in pregnancy reduces the residual risk of mother-to-child transmission (MTCT), when infants also receive standard timely hepatitis-B vaccination (and hepatitis-B immune globulin where used).

**Why this works:** Transmission despite infant immunoprophylaxis is concentrated among mothers with very high viraemia. TDF powerfully lowers maternal HBV DNA before delivery, reducing infant exposure.

**Key evidence:** A pivotal randomized trial enrolled 200 highly viraemic, HBeAg-positive pregnant women and began TDF at 30–32 weeks’ gestation. It found substantially less infant HBV infection than no maternal antiviral therapy, alongside markedly lower maternal viral load at delivery. The trial is the basis for later guideline recommendations.  
https://www.peeref.com/works/2920881  
http://www.corevih-bretagne.fr/ckfinder/userfiles/files/Congrès/CROI_2017/Articles_Mercredi_15/Pan+et+al_+-+2016+-+Tenofovir+to+Prevent+Hepatitis+B+Transmission+in+M.pdf

**Guidelines and synthesis:** WHO recommends TDF from week 28 until at least delivery for HBsAg-positive women with HBV DNA ≥200,000 IU/mL. A later systematic review/meta-analysis of antiviral prophylaxis in pregnancy also supports reduced MTCT, while safety follow-up remains important.  
https://www.aidsdatahub.org/sites/default/files/resource/who-pmtct-hepatitis-b-virus-2020.pdf  
https://www.hepatitisb.uw.edu/go/prevention-hbv/preventing-perinatal-transmission-hbv/core-concept/all

This is prophylaxis for high viral load, not a substitute for infant birth-dose vaccination. Treatment decisions, timing of stopping postpartum, maternal liver indications, and infant follow-up should be managed by obstetric/hepatitis specialists.
